Building on this foundation, we continue to strengthen our coordinated response. And actively promotes healthy lifestyles, including through balanced diets such as the Mediterranean diet. In this context, Italy intends to reiterate its position and willingness to continue collaborating on this issue at the international level, while at the same time ensuring the need to safeguard the sovereignty of states in matters of public health and taxation. Therefore, we oppose any prescriptive language that grants international organizations the authority to adopt or impose measures in these areas. Italy also opposes front-of-pack labelling systems that could provide consumers with misleading information, and favours informative rather than directive labels, more effective in raising awareness and ultimately improving consumer behaviour. Regarding alcoholic beverages, Italy supports public awareness campaigns against the abuse of these products and in favor to a responsible consumption. But we do not.

Support any equivalence between tobacco and alcoholic beverages and any language that recommends policies to counter responsible consumption of alcoholic.

Beverages. Italy promotes a correct and effective information on the prevention and treatment of non-communicable diseases. But we do not support measures that could limit the freedom of speech, including on this matter. Keeping in mind these principles, Italy looks forward to continuing working together with other nations to reduce non-communicable diseases risk factors, promote mental health, and well-being.

Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Italy. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Islamic Republic of Iran.

Madam Vice President, Excellencies, non-communicable diseases are complex, multidimensional, and costly, requiring effective and timely prevention through social accountability, literacy promotion, and collaboration. Tackling NCDs depend on accurate data, context-specific action plans, appropriate technologies, and above all, strong political commitments. Iran has responded through the establishment of the National and City Committee, INCDC, chaired by the Minister of Health and Medical Education, which develops national and provincial plans for early detection, management, monitoring, and risk reduction. Our unique health governance system, where the medical education has been merged into health services within the Ministry of Health and Medical Education, has created a functional mechanism for cost-effective and in-house training of service providers who are able to conduct world-class biomedical research on NCDs, including national and subnational burden of disease studies and timely national NCD surveillance mechanisms. At the global level, combating NCDs demands multilateralism and solidarity. Key principles include, first, political commitment at the highest level and across all sectors of development. Second, strengthened and resilient health systems with equitable access to affordable, safe, and quality medicines and technology. Third, addressing risk factors, social determinants, and international determinants of health, notably indiscriminate health sector targeted UCMs that violate people's right to health. The right to development encompassing equitable and unhindered access to economic progress and social well-being is a cornerstone of the global fight against NCDs. Robust and unconditional technology transfer is imperative, particularly for developing countries. We need to underline that UCMs pose severe threat to global health, disrupting supply chains, procurement, limiting access to medical supplies, and hindering the ability of nations to meet their health and development goals. These measures are contrary to the principles of the United Nations Charter and the spirit of international cooperation and solidarity. Unilateral coercive measures are unlawful, illegitimate, and profoundly harmful. The Islamic Republic of Iran demands that repressive actions be recognized for that they are violations of the right to health and obstacles to our collective commitments on NCDs and well-being. We call for their immediate removal. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

President, Health is humanity's eternal pursuit and the foundation and purpose of development. China commends the efforts of the Secretariat, the WHO, and all parties in organizing this meeting and supports the political declaration adopted by the meeting. Always putting people and their lives first, China implements a health-first development strategy, advances universal health coverage, and has built the world's largest healthcare system. significantly improving the health of its people. We attach great importance to the prevention and control of NCDs and the promotion of mental health, advancing them in an integrated manner as key measures in implementing the Healthy China strategy. We have launched medium and long-term actions to prevent and control NCDs and promote mental health, further improve the equity and accessibility of relevant health services. President global public health governance faces new challenges, NCDs and mental health have become global issues of wide concern for governments and societies. This requires us to strengthen political commitment and take collective action. China calls on all parties to fully recognize the importance and urgency of preventing and controlling NCDs and improving mental health, to increase investment in relevant areas, and to effectively reduce relevant threats and risks. At the same time, we support the WHO in playing a leading and coordinating role in relevant areas and in carrying out extensive international cooperation, technical exchange, and external assistance within multilateral frameworks such as the United Nations and to jointly address global health challenges. Not long ago, Chinese President Xi Jinping put forward the global governance initiative. China will continue to uphold the vision of a global community of health for all, strengthen exchanges and cooperation with the international community in the prevention and control of NCDs and mental health promotion, improve service models, enhance equity in health, jointly safeguard human health and well-being and global public health security, and reform and improve global governance system. Thank you, President.
I thank the distinguished representative of China, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Sudan.

Thank you, Madam President. My delegation is pleased to participate in the fourth high-level meeting of the General Assembly on the prevention and control of NCDs, the achievement of justice and inclusiveness and the promotion of mental health and public well-being. We support consensus on the political declaration. We hope that this document and its predecessors a realistic and real political commitment to implement practical steps that will promote fruitful cooperation. It would be remiss not to thank the facilitators of the political declaration for their effort. We would like to thank the permanent delegation of Iraq as head of the Group of 77 and China for their wise and successful leadership. Madam President, distinguished participants, For the development and well-being of peoples, we have to provide health services in a fair and equitable manner, it has to be accessible and cost effective for all. For this meeting to be a real transformative moment, the international community must have a genuine desire to strengthen and deepen international cooperation. We have to work constructively to eliminate all obstacles that stand in the face of development. We have to ensure the equitable and unhindered access to health technologies and preventive measures and treatment. We need to find ways to cooperate to overcome financial obstacles while supporting research and scientific innovations. This will strengthen all, especially developing countries, in accordance with their own priorities. To conclude, Madam President, Sudan makes concerted and continuous effort to expand healthcare coverage and provide healthcare to all citizens. This includes diagnostic and treatment services. However, as a result of the war of aggression led by the rapid support militias that garner regional support. Sudan's health systems operate in a very challenging environment. This poses additional burden on the health systems. The complexities associated with the war led to shortages of the basic necessities of life. There is an increasing demand for health services. This led to a hard humanitarian situation. However, the Federal Ministry of Health and the Humanitarian Aid Commission, the private sector institutions in cooperation with civil society organizations are making all effort possible in coordination with the UN agencies to fill the gaps and provide the necessary health and preventive services. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Sudan, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of El Salvador.

Thank you very much, Madam President. El Salvador recognizes the importance of this debate and reaffirms that health is not just a service, it is a fundamental right and also a pillar for sustainable development. My country has shouldered this commitment through the implementation of the comprehensive policy on non-communicable diseases. It articulates a multi-sectoral strategic plan. Within this framework, we have deployed the HEARTS strategy in all primary care facilities, guaranteeing early diagnosis and access to treatment for cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease. This has allowed us to reduce by 11%. premature mortality by NCDs and to significantly improve our control indices for hypertension and diabetes. In the fight against cervical and uterine cancer, we have achieved a vaccine rate against HPV of more than 80% in girls. We are also expanding screening and treatment and also incorporating innovative technologies such as thermocoagulation for precancerous lesions, thus achieving a reduction in mortality of 34.6%. The digitalization of the healthcare system, Madam President, has been key. Today, we have an electronic patient history for 100% of services. This allows us to carry out effective follow-up of all patients. Moreover, we have added the inclusion of nutrition, exercise, and prevention programs within the community. Moreover, we have taken the historic step of carrying out the first national mental health survey. It strengthens the care for children, adolescents and perinatal women, making sure that mental health is no longer an invisible subject, Madam President. This progress reflects the conviction that no global health target can be reached without prioritizing equity, prevention, and access, which really need to be universal. El Salvador thus today reaffirms its firm commitment to work together with all of you, the international community, to make sure that health and well-being can be a reality for all, for all persons. wherever they may be. Thank you very much, Madam President.
I thank the distinguished representative of El Salvador. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Lithuania.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, health is the foundation of dignity and prosperity. Yet today, non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular illness, diabetes, and chronic respiratory conditions remain the leading cause of death in Europe. They account for two-thirds of death and 77% of disease burden. Beyond the numbers, they weaken communities and cost our economies billions each year. Yet we know that much of this can be prevented by tackling the risk factors of tobacco, alcohol, unhealthy diets, and inactivity. Alongside this, we must also address mental health. In recent years, it has rightly gained greater recognition as an essential part of overall well-being. Yet, many countries still face serious challenges from stigma and low funding to rising mental illness. In Lithuania, one in eight citizens has a diagnosed mental or behavioral disorder. Additionally, for many years, we carried the tragic distinction of having the highest suicide rate in Europe. This has been one of the greatest national challenges, but through steady effort, awareness, and reform, we cut the rate in half over the last decade. We have also raised funding and placed mental health closer to the core of our health system. Today, we are implementing comprehensive reforms. We are shifting from hospital-based to community-based service. guiding by human rights and recovery principles. We are expanding psychotherapy and crisis response teams, introducing new suicide prevention tools, and building a network of mental health ambassadors to fight stigma. By 2030, Lithuania has set ambitious yet clear targets to reduce suicide by 40 percent, decrease hospitalizations by one third, lower stigma, and cut substance abuse among young people by nearly 30 percent. Finally, Lithuania is also pursuing a new strategic direction, integrating mental health into all policies. Excellencies, the statement is simple. Non-communicable diseases and mental health together define the well-being of our societies. Both require prevention, innovation, and equity. Both demand stronger international cooperation and active involvement of civil society. And both must be addressed with urgency if we are to save lives, reduce inequality, and build healthier, fairer societies. Health is not simply the absence of disease. It is the foundation of opportunity, dignity, and peace. Let us commit to building a future where every person can live with health, dignity, and hope. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Lithuania. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malaysia.

Madam President, Malaysia reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and Global NCD Monitoring Framework. We recognise that the rising burden of non-communicable diseases and mental health condition is not only a public health crisis, but also a profound threat to economic growth, social well-being and national resilience. The high-level meeting today places a spotlight on an urgent need for leadership and coordinated action to deliver meaningful transformation. In this regard, Malaysia strongly supports the approval of the Political Declaration on NCDs and Mental Health at this meeting, recognising it as a vital step towards strengthening international cooperation and reaffirming our shared responsibility to safeguard health for all. Building on this global commitment, Malaysia national policy direction is firmly anchored in evidence-based planning and multi-sectoral collaboration. The National Strategic Plan for NCDs, the National Oral Health Strategic Plan 2022-2030, the National Strategic Plan for Mental Health 2020-2025, and the Health White Paper collectively serve as our strategic blueprints for prevention, early detection, integrated management, and system.

Reform.

This framework aligns national priorities with global commitments, ensuring quality, accountability, and sustainability. Malaysia adopts a life-course approach in addressing NCDs and mental health, ensuring that prevention and care span from.

Early life to old age.

Our efforts cover the full continuum of prevention as follows: Primordial and primary prevention is advanced through the intersectoral policies on tobacco control, mental health promotion and early crisis intervention, national campaigns, nutrition, oral health and physical activity, as well as community-based programmes that create enabling environments for healthier living. At the secondary level, the National Health Screening Initiative strengthens systemic early detection and timely intervention support, supported by robust national surveillance and registries. And at the tertiary level, structured care pathways are being enhanced, including the integration of psychosocial rehabilitation services at primary healthcare facilities.

Malaysia's efforts are underpinned by the whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach, bringing together ministries, civil societies, academia.

Communities and the private sector to build synergies and foster innovation. Through technology, stronger surveillance and innovation driven by strategic partnerships, we aim to expand accessibility and reinforce sustainability. Malaysia reaffirms its steadfast commitment to build a healthier, more resilient and more productive nation. We will continue to invest in transformative leadership, integrated action, and global solidarity in pursuit of the sustainable development goals.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia. I now give the floor to the Distinguished Representative of Sri Lanka.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates. I wish to express Sri Lanka's appreciation for convening this timely meeting under the theme, "Equity and Integration: Transforming Lives and Livelihoods through Leadership and Action on Non-Communicable Diseases and the Promotion of Mental Health and Well-Being," that calls for shared commitment, collective action, and renewed resolve to address the pressing challenges of NCDs. According to the World Health Organization, non-communicable diseases, or NCDs, account for nearly 74% of all deaths worldwide. These include conditions such as heart disease, stroke, cancer, diabetes, and chronic respiratory diseases. Alarmingly, an estimated 86% of premature deaths and more than three-quarters of all NCD-related deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries. The causes are closely linked to mental health challenges that remain under-treated and under-funded. The cost is measured not only in human lives, but in lost productivity, widened inequities and in strained health systems. In Sri Lanka, non-communicable diseases present a significant health challenge. The leading causes of NCD-related deaths are cardiovascular disease, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases, and diabetes mellitus, with cardiovascular diseases remaining the forefront contributor to mortality. With our population undergoing demographic transition and a growing aging segment, the burden of NCD is expected to rise further. As a developing nation, we face numerous challenges in combating these diseases. Unhealthy lifestyle behaviors such as excessive alcohol consumption, tobacco use, physical inactivity, and poor dietary habits remain significant risks. Our challenge is to encourage citizens to move away from entrenched sedentary lifestyles and to adopt healthier habits. Sri Lanka has long recognized that prevention and care for non-communicable diseases can be more effectively delivered through primary health care. To this end, we have established more than 1,000 healthy lifestyle centers across the country offering screening for cardiovascular risk, hypertension, and diabetes. The Government recognises the importance of increasing awareness among the public of the value of early detection and preventive healthcare. Efforts are under way to encourage greater participation in screening programmes in that regard. As we consider this timely matter today, it is important that we acknowledge the challenges in many countries, including our own, in guaranteeing.
I thank the representative of Sri Lanka, and I now give the floor to the representative of Republic of Moldova.

Madam President, it is an honor to address the high-level meeting and to reaffirm the commitment of the Republic of Moldova to advancing of the global agenda of non-communicable diseases and mental health. We meet at the decisive moment. Non-communicable diseases and mental health conditions remain among the greatest public health challenges of our time, driving inequities and threatening sustainable development. Moldova has made the prevention and control of NCDs, as well as the promotion of mental health and well-being, a national priority. Through our national programme of prevention and control of priority NCDs for 2023-2027 and the Health 2030 strategy, we aim to reduce premature mortality by strengthening public health capacities, addressing behavioural risk factors, and ensuring that prevention is central to our response. In recent years, Moldova has achieved a notable reduction in suicide mortality, reflecting both policy commitment and social change. Our National Mental Health Program 2023-2027 is designed to strengthen community-based services, reduce stigma, and ensure that psychological resilience is built into our health system. During 2020's second refugee crisis, we witnessed firsthand the importance of multi-sectoral cooperation, border police, social workers, educators, and civil society working together to provide immediate support and counseling to those in distress. This experience taught us that protection mental health is not only a medical matter, but a collective responsibility across all sectors. Yet, we recognize that no country can achieve these outcomes alone. This is why Moldova has embraced the principle of health in all policies. Through strategic partnership, we are scaling up initiatives such as health-promoting schools and healthy communities, while also building sustainable models of integrated medical and social service, particularly in rural areas. With the support of development partners, the Healthy Life project and the Mensana program are driving progress in both NCDs care and mental health reform, showcasing the impact of long-term, multi-sectoral collaboration. Excellencies, looking forward, we must ensure that integrated, people-centered NCDs and mental health services are embedded in universal.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Republic of Moldova, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malawi.

Madam President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, The Republic of Malawi welcomes this timely high-level meeting and commends the UN for placing equity and integration at the head of global response to NCDs and mental health. These dual challenges are not only public health concerns, but pressing development, equity, and resilience issues. In Malawi, NCDs now account for 40% of all deaths, with hypertension affecting 33% of adults and diabetes over 6%. Cervical cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths amongst women, whilst rheumatic heart disease, epilepsy, and asthma continue to burden our health system. Mental health conditions are also rising sharply, with suicide rates at 11.6 per 100,000 in 2022, and common disorders such as depression and anxiety are widespread, yet services remain centralized and underfunded. Despite these challenges, Malawi has made important strides. Through the national NCD strategy and mental health policy, we are integrating services into the essential health package. scaling up screening and treatment at the primary care level, and expanding pain plus clinics for chronic care. The new Mental Health Act of 2025 modernizes outdated legislation and decriminalizing suicide and decentralizing services, while the National Suicide Prevention Framework and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support Task Force are advancing cross-sector coordination. Community-led models, such as the friendship bench and interpersonal group therapies, are expanding psychosocial support, while digital tools like the Diabetes Compass, strengthening surveillance, patient tracking, and continuity of care. This progress has been achieved despite climate shocks, humanitarian emergencies, and a limited fiscal space. Cyclone Freddy in 2023 exposed the fragility of chronic care systems in Malawi, but we responded by training over 3,500, uh, psychological first aid providers and 367 group therapy facilitators. who have reached more than 1 million vulnerable people. These experiences reinforce our resolve to integrate NCDs and mental health services into emergency preparedness and also invest in climate-resilient health facilities, digitized records, and mobile outreach to safeguard continuity of care. Madam President, to accelerate progress, Malawi calls on the global community to scale up catalytic financing for integrated NCDs and mental health. support workforce development, strengthen supply chain for essential medicines, diagnostics, and digital innovations, and invest in robust data systems, including within pandemic preparedness frameworks. Malawi remains resolute to achieving SDG 3 and the commitments of this political declaration. Let us together act with compassion.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malawi, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nepal.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, it is a privilege to join you all at this timely meeting. Nepal aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of Group of 77 and China. Excellencies, today, global non-communicable disease and mental health governance is at a crossroad. Non-communicable disease continue to claim two-thirds of global deaths and about 71% of total deaths in Nepal. Mental health issues are a serious public concern, and vulnerable communities in developing countries, particularly LDCs, are among the most affected. Quality, accessible, and affordable healthcare remains at the core of our public health governance. It is a cornerstone of a healthy life and a driver for sustainable development. In Nepal, every citizen enjoys emergency and free basic healthcare as a fundamental right. The national health policy aligns with the SDGs, including reducing premature death from NCDs, expanding universal health services, and prioritizing mental health well-being. For ensuring social justice, marginalized communities are integrated into the social health protection system. Initiatives like Mother, Golden 1000 Days, free dialysis services, and cash support have reduced maternal and child mortality while preventing non-communicable diseases. At we face daunting challenges, systemic barriers, financial constraints, inadequate health professionals and infrastructure, fragmented policies, and health literacy, among others. Excellencies, globally, over a billion people suffer from mental health disorders. About 4% of Nepali adults are estimated to be battling with mental health problems. Rising conflicts. climate catastrophe, unhealthy lifestyles, economic disparities have added oods. Mental health is often stigmatized. This has profound socioeconomic consequences for individuals, economies, and nations. Let me highlight a strategic focus on three pillars. First, we must ensure healthy, healthy, health equity by providing reliable, affordable, and accessible health care to all, regardless of their socioeconomic status. Second, integration approach should prioritize aligning NCD and mental health with primary health services. This requires digital health solutions, community involvement, adequate funding, capacity building, and global partnerships. Third, increased official development assistance, technology transfer, and capacity building support from development partners to developing countries, particularly LDCs, are crucial for implementing preventive, curative, and awareness-raising initiatives in the NCD and mental health space. Fourth, strengthening public health insurance and ensuring protection, especially to vulnerable communities, is essential. Additionally, a whole of society and whole of multi-stakeholder cooperation is needed to break silos for impactful change. Together, we can build a healthier, resilient, and.
I thank the distinguished representative of Nepal. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of France.

Madam President, ladies and gentlemen, non-communicable diseases and mental health are a major challenge for global public health. They account for 70 percent of deaths around the world, and there's a need for unprecedented mobilization. We know only prevention will allow us to reduce their devastating impact on millions of lives. We call for the adoption of the political declaration. France would like to see this to be a more ambitious text, but even so, this declaration reflects the urgency of acting, and for the first time, states that mental health is an essential component of global health, defining individual and collective well-being, We must move from commitments to results with rigorous follow-up measures and specific actions that would be efficient. To get there, France will work side by side with the UN, the WHO, and special agencies. We call for the training of global personnel capable of assisting states in investing in policies of prevention, education, health, specifically through the World Health Organization Academy. On the regional level in Europe, France closely works with its partners to develop joint prevention programs targeting risk factors. This approach makes it possible to adapt policies to local realities while harmonizing efforts to maximize their effectiveness. On the national level, France has launched an ambitious public health plan. Our strategy is based on a multi-sectoral approach linking education, environment, and health. Prevention begins at the earliest age and continues throughout a person's lifetime through awareness raising campaigns, follow up, promotion of healthy lifestyles, and early screening. Mental health in particular occupies a central place in that agenda. It has been designated the great national course in France for 2025. But prevention cannot be just a domain of governments. We must mobilize all actors, civil society, academia, private sector, health professionals, and the citizens themselves. The fight against non-communicable diseases and mental health is a long-term fight.
I thank the distinguished representative of France, and now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Israel.

Thank you, Madam President. Noncommunicable diseases stand as one of the defining health challenges of our time. Prevention is the most powerful tool we possess. It saves resources, and more importantly, it saves lives. Taking this responsibility further, we should ensure that global health is not only defined by years added to life, but by life lived with health, well-being, and dignity. This requires cultivating environments that encourage healthy choices and lifestyles, encompassing nutrition and physical activity, as well as strengthening systems for early detection and active management of NCDs. Israel strongly encourages international cooperation to prioritize the most impactful areas of intervention, such as cancer and diabetes, where meaningful progress can be made. Madam President, among the non-communicable diseases, mental health must be fully integrated into comprehensive health systems with dedicated resources, reliable data monitoring, and accountability mechanisms. These services must reach marginalized groups, minorities, and all those most likely not to receive help in times of crisis in order to leave no one behind. It is regrettable that certain delegations chose to continually and cynically politicize this forum today while ignoring reality on the ground. After the October 7 attacks, Israel was marked with a profound national trauma, with over 200,000 civilians displaced and thousands directly exposed to violence and loss. In such moments, the need for mental health services is immediate and profound. Our line centers spread across the country became places of healing and strength, offering therapy and equipping communities to face crisis together. Digital tools continue to play a role, a central role in the teletherapy consultations offered free by Israel's national healthcare system. This enables prompt and consistent care to dispersed and displaced populations, providing example of scalable solutions. Israel also emphasizes holistic rehabilitation, linking physical and psychological treatment as an inseparable part of recovery for affected populations and returned hostages. Madam President, we also recognize the essential duty to protect those on the front lines of response. Israel's established services to support emergency personnel, medical teams, and hospital staff treating traumatized survivors and hostages. Sustained investment is required for the long journey of recovery to prevent trauma from evolving into chronic suffering. Israel remains committed to sharing its experience in NCD prevention and treatment, trauma care, and emergency mental health preparedness as just one part of its drive to strengthen collective resilience and ensure that no individual and no member state faces these challenges alone. I thank you, Madam President.

I thank the distinguished representative of Israel. We have now exhausted the time available to us for the plenary segment of the high-level meeting of the General Assembly on non-communicable diseases and the promotion of mental health well-being. Unfortunately, we still have several delegations who requested the floor and were not able to make their statement owing to time constraints. I would encourage those delegations to submit their statements to e-statements@un.org for posting on the UN Journal. The closing segment of the high-level meeting will take place immediately following the conclusion of this plenary segment. Please remain seated. We will now begin the closing segment of the high-level meeting of the General Assembly on non-communicable diseases and the promotion of mental health and well-being. Heads of state and government, ministers, excellencies, distinguished delegates, distinguished participants, I would like to express my appreciation to all participants and warmly congratulate the co-chairs of the multi-stakeholder panels for their outstanding leadership. Pursuant to Assembly resolution 79/273, I now invite Ms. Cornelia Sanchez a WHO Civil Society Working Group on NCDs, a lawyer, bioethics, African health justice campaigner, and lived experience expert to deliver a statement.

Madam President, distinguished delegates, fellow citizens living with NCDs and mental health conditions globally, Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your earnest deliberations on the catastrophic burden of non-communicable diseases and mental health conditions today. Thank you for the new political declaration adopted that offers stronger targets on tobacco control, mental health, access to medicines, and support for lived experience. The statistics on the mortalities and mobilities are grim. The human suffering, indignities, and the health inequities caused by noncommunicable diseases and mental health are unconscionable. My job before you today in this august house is not to repeat the numbers or to warn you of the catastrophic financial costs of NCDs and mental health conditions to domestic and global economies. My job here today is to be the face and the upholder of the health and human rights of the hundreds of millions of peoples living with NCDs and mental health conditions globally. I use the term peoples to capture the size and diversity of my global lived experience, patient partner community. I am a South African citizen. in remission for breast cancer, and I am living with bipolar mood disorder and chemotherapy-induced congestive heart failure. Your Excellencies, please allow me to share the scale of human suffering caused by NCDs and mental health conditions. I have lost and buried three loved ones to NCDs and mental health conditions since the 14th of July, 2025. The last funeral I attended was on the 9th of September, 2025, when we buried a beautiful, funny, kind, super talented young African. He was 26 years old. I almost lost another beloved African man to mental health six days before his 34th birthday on the 11th of September 2025. He would have been my fourth loss to NCDs and mental health conditions since the 14th of July 2025, he would have been the second death by suicide due to mental health. I am thankful to the universe and to his medical team that he is still with us and that he is recovering in hospital. while I am here. Your Excellencies, my lived experience is not a reflection of sheer bad luck or of human failing. My family, friends, and I are not unique in our mental and physical exhaustion and human suffering. Millions are also suffering in distant corners of the world, especially on my continent, Africa, and other low to middle income regions. And of course, in the hot searing conflict areas like Palestine, like Gaza. Your Excellencies, I am here to invite us all to intentionally seize this moment of the new political declaration. I invite us to legally and morally recommit ourselves to addressing the global burden of NCDs and mental health conditions. We can do this three ways. First, I implore us to change the language we use to talk about NCDs and mental health conditions. I ask you to replace the phrase people living with NCDs, with citizens living with NCDs. I invoke the language of citizenship to describe my community because it confers rights and obligations for us as health users. I use the language of citizenship because it also confers legal duties on you, your excellencies, as state parties of the United Nations, it imposes on you the obligation to respect, protect, promote, and fulfill the fundamental health and human rights and other interrelated health rights of us people living with NCDs. I correct myself, citizens living with NCDs. It also confers on us citizens living with NCDs the human right to participate as lived experience, experts, and as civil society members in the development, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of national, regional, and global decisions and policies that affect our lives. Part of your duty, your excellencies, to respect, protect, promote and fulfil includes the responsibility to legally ensure that third parties do not infringe on your citizens' fundamental health and human rights. I implore you, therefore, to introduce and enforce stringent regulations to prevent the wanton health harms of the alcohol, fast foods, and tobacco industries. I implore you, secondly, to commit to sustainable financing for NCDs and mental health prevention and control at nation state, regional level, and global levels. I am aware of national, regional, and global financial crisis. aggravated by geopolitics, especially since the 20th of January 2025. I am consciously aware of the ramifications of the financial costs to global health funding and how they have impacted access to regular, safe, affordable essential medicines and treatments, especially for predominantly black and brown people in Africa and the global south. I am encouraged by your express inclusion of lived experience support, sorry, lived experience experts in the political declaration. Your Excellencies, I, however, want to respectfully caution you against falling into declarationist nominalism, like the late Pope Francis warned you during his September 2015 United Nations address. You cannot substantively include lived experience experts like myself and civil society organization without meaningful financial and knowledge resource investment. The realization of human rights like the health users' right to participate requires financial investment and unflinching political will moral commitment to citizens living with NCDs and mental health from head of states working together with ministers of finance, health, and the whole of government. In conclusion, your excellencies, may I remind you of the key two principles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. That is, they are universal. That means they are for everyone, everywhere. Secondly, let me remind you of the principle of non-discrimination, which means you cannot unjustifiably limit human rights. NCDs, contrary to our global health policymaking and political discourses, NCDs and mental health conditions are not invincible. They are not silent killers, and they are not lifestyle diseases. They are disabling, life-threatening, impoverishing, public health threats like HIV and COVID-19. Your Excellencies, non-communicable diseases and mental health conditions deserve your urgent action. They deserve your political will, and they deserve sustained financing. I thank you.

I thank Ms. Asante. Allow me now to summarize the discussions held during the multi-stakeholder panels and to deliver concluding remarks. Ms. Asante, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, we have reached the close of this high-level meeting on non-communicable diseases and mental health. I thank all Member States and stakeholders for their active engagement and for reaffirming that tackling NCDs is central to achieving the SDGs.
